questions.prompt: What problem is clustering primarily used to solve in these notes?

choices.text: Predicting labels from previously labeled examples.
choices.response: Incorrect. That is the framing of supervised classification, not clustering.

choices.text: Discovering natural groupings in unlabeled data by identifying shared patterns in features.
choices.response: Correct. The note defines clustering as discovering structure in unlabeled data through shared feature patterns.

choices.text: Compressing every dataset into a single aggregate summary statistic.
choices.response: Incorrect. Clustering reveals group-level structure rather than collapsing everything into one summary.

choices.text: Cleaning missing values and resolving inconsistencies before analysis.
choices.response: Incorrect. That is preparation work that supports clustering, not clustering itself.

questions.explanation: The note presents clustering as the task of discovering natural groupings in unlabeled data by identifying shared patterns in features.

questions.prompt: Why do these notes emphasize data quality and EDA before applying a clustering algorithm?

choices.text: Because clustering automatically fixes missing values and noisy records during training.
choices.response: Incorrect. The article says poor data can directly distort the patterns clustering tries to uncover.

choices.text: Because EDA and cleaning help reveal outliers, noise, and suspicious structure before they mislead the clustering result.
choices.response: Correct. The note explicitly says EDA helps surface issues early so the discovered clusters are more trustworthy.

choices.text: Because clustering only works after the data is manually labeled by domain experts.
choices.response: Incorrect. Clustering is useful precisely because it works on unlabeled data.

choices.text: Because every clustering method requires the same preprocessing pipeline regardless of the data.
choices.response: Incorrect. The point is not identical preprocessing for all methods, but protecting structure from distortion.

questions.explanation: EDA and data cleaning matter because missing values, noise, and inconsistencies can distort the structure clustering is supposed to recover.

questions.prompt: According to the note, what makes two objects count as close in clustering?

choices.text: They are always physically near each other in a two-dimensional plot.
choices.response: Incorrect. The note stresses that closeness is not automatically physical distance.

choices.text: They share the same label assigned by a classification model.
choices.response: Incorrect. Clustering is defined before labels exist.

choices.text: They are close under the chosen representation and similarity or distance measure.
choices.response: Correct. The note argues that clustering only becomes meaningful after representation and similarity are made explicit.

choices.text: They contain the same number of raw features, regardless of feature meaning.
choices.response: Incorrect. Feature count alone does not define similarity.

questions.explanation: In these notes, closeness depends on how objects are represented and what similarity or distance measure is chosen.

questions.prompt: Which clustering family is presented as especially useful for irregular cluster shapes and outliers?

choices.text: Centroid-based methods such as K-Means.
choices.response: Incorrect. The note says centroid-based methods work best when clusters are compact and center-shaped.

choices.text: Density-based methods such as DBSCAN.
choices.response: Correct. The note highlights DBSCAN for irregular shapes and cases where outliers should remain noise.

choices.text: Hierarchical methods such as AGNES and DIANA.
choices.response: Incorrect. Hierarchical methods focus on nested structure across different levels of granularity.

choices.text: Rule-based classification methods.
choices.response: Incorrect. That is not one of the clustering families discussed here.

questions.explanation: Density-based methods such as DBSCAN are emphasized for irregular shapes and for treating outliers as noise.

questions.prompt: What is the defining idea behind hierarchical clustering in these notes?

choices.text: Every cluster must be summarized by a single centroid.
choices.response: Incorrect. That is the centroid-based view.

choices.text: Clusters are dense regions connected through local neighborhoods.
choices.response: Incorrect. That is the density-based view.

choices.text: Clusters are nested groupings that can be examined at multiple levels of granularity.
choices.response: Correct. The note defines hierarchical methods as building a hierarchy rather than a single flat partition.

choices.text: Clusters only exist when a dataset is already labeled into classes.
choices.response: Incorrect. Labels are not required for clustering.

questions.explanation: Hierarchical clustering is presented as a nested structure that supports multiple levels of grouping rather than one flat partition.
